headings: Goals by the licence they need
links: Re-scan
Open the step →
sentences: Based on the scan from this minute · <date and time>.
Re-scan
IAMAI hardens what the tenant has.
Every goal is scored against the best implementation the licence allows.
Goals that need a missing tier are listed for reference, never as an accepted gap.
Every user satisfies MFA on every app
Admins use phishing-resistant auth
Admin portals need strong auth or are blocked for non-admins
Guests satisfy MFA
Security-info registration requires a trusted context
Legacy protocols blocked
Device-code flow blocked
Authentication transfer blocked
Sign-ins outside allowed countries blocked
Admin sessions expire quickly and never persist
Unmanaged-device browser sessions are limited
Office apps require a compliant or joined device
Unknown platforms blocked
Mobile access requires approved or protected apps
Azure management requires strong auth
Registering or joining a device requires MFA
Windows desktop sessions require token protection
Browser sessions never persist for anyone
Unmanaged devices cannot download
: When Microsoft says a sign-in looks risky, demand MFA or block it automatically.
: A likely-compromised account must change its password through a secured flow.
: Elevating to an admin role should always cost a fresh MFA, even mid-session.
: Medium sign-in risk is common enough to matter; MFA clears most of it without blocking anyone.
: A medium-risk user is likely compromised: force a secure password change.
: Service principals can be scoped and risk-gated too (Workload ID Premium).
: Device enrollment is a trust boundary — make it a fresh, interactive sign-in.
The spine of every plan, regardless of licence: curated from Microsoft guidance.
Rungs without a link are done outside Conditional Access, in the settings each one names.
: Microsoft's free baseline: MFA for admins, MFA registration for everyone, legacy authentication blocked.
The starting point when there is no Conditional Access.
: Two cloud-only emergency accounts, excluded from every policy and signed in on a schedule, so a mistaken policy still leaves a way back in.
: Find every sign-in that still uses basic authentication (POP, IMAP, SMTP, ActiveSync) before it can be blocked.
: App passwords bypass MFA; move the apps that use them to modern authentication and turn the feature off.
: Legacy per-user MFA fights with Conditional Access and security defaults; set every user to disabled there before policies take over.
: Admin roles on a mailbox-holding account make every phishing email a tenant-wide risk; give admins a second, role-only account.
: Two to four Global Administrators is Microsoft's guidance; everyone else gets the least role that does their job.
: Remove guests nobody sponsors and invitations never accepted; what remains is what guest policies protect.
: An account nobody uses is an account nobody notices being used; disable after 90 days of silence.
: Text and call codes are the weakest tier; the verification campaign moves people to Microsoft Authenticator or passkeys.

surfaces.name: Naming policies and groups
headings: A worked example from this tenant
sentences: Explains the naming convention behind every name IAMAI proposes, and how it reads the one this tenant already uses.
A Conditional Access policy name is the only thing an admin sees in a list of forty.
A good one answers three questions without opening it: who it applies to, what it does, and whether it is on purpose.
The convention below is a common one, not the only one.
What matters is that a tenant picks one and holds to it.
Prefix.
Groups policies that belong to one set, so they sort together and a stranger can tell yours from Microsoft’s.
Scope.
Who it applies to: Global, Admins, Guests, or a persona.
Action.
Block, Require, Grant, or Session.
Target.
The thing being protected or restricted.
Core - Global - Block - Legacy authentication
Core - Admins - Require - Phishing-resistant MFA
Core - Exclusion - Break-glass
Core - Pilot - MFA enforcement
Core - Exception - Legacy service accounts
An exclusion group’s name should make its risk obvious.
Anyone reading Core - Exclusion - Break-glass knows the members sit outside the policies, which is the point of naming it that way.
Core - Trusted - Head office
Core - Allowed countries
100% of the 3 policy names here follow CA<n> - <...>, so IAMAI proposes names in that shape rather than its own.
A policy this plan creates: CA004 - Require phishing-resistant MFA for admins Matches this tenant
The exclusion group this plan creates: CA005 - Break-glass exclusions Matches this tenant
A named location this plan creates: CA006 - Trusted head office Matches this tenant
Renaming a policy changes no evaluation.
Nobody is affected, nothing needs a report-only window, and it can be undone by renaming it back.
Consolidating two policies into one is a different thing entirely and follows the six stages on that step.
